strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring foundation-model representations into a compact detector for few-shot personal object recognition. The separation between offline distillation and teacher-free personalization is practically motivated.

Table 2 reports meaningful improvements across four datasets. MOCHA initialized from AuXFT improves the seven-column average from 53.8 to 58.7 and exceeds AuXFT in every reported setting. The COCO-initialized variant also improves the average to 56.0.

The experiments provide useful component evidence. Table 1 supports combining visual and language-conditioned features, while Table 3 shows benefits from the relational loss and translator attention. The appendix provides additional compression experiments and paired significance tests.
The manuscript acknowledges its closest predecessor, AuXFT, and explains the intended differences. It also candidly discusses training cost and limitations when scaling personalization.
weaknesses: The central teacher representation is not specified consistently enough to reproduce. Section 4.1 describes LLaVA-1.5-7B as using CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard model uses ViT-L/14. Section 3.2 applies the same projection to visual and textual embeddings without explaining dimensional compatibility, and Algorithm A.1 computes h_i from the class label alone, omitting the image conditioning central to the method. The exact checkpoint, hidden-state layer, pooled token positions, and generation procedure are needed to establish what supervision actually produced the results.

Important implementation details for the new components are missing. The paper does not report the loss weights, temperature, translator dimensions or attention configuration. Equation 7 does not specify whether self-distances are masked before softmax, although Equation 8 excludes diagonal terms; these alternatives define different objectives. The appendix also describes channel normalization as preceding PCA, contrary to Equations 2–3. Referring to AuXFT's settings does not resolve these method-specific ambiguities.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the contribution beyond stronger teacher features and additional training. The strongest model starts from an already distilled AuXFT checkpoint and receives another 20 epochs. A matched continuation of AuXFT, and AuXFT trained with the same CLIP or fused teacher targets, would help distinguish the benefit of MOCHA's formulation from initialization, teacher choice, and training budget. The reported gains remain encouraging, but their attribution is incomplete.

The abstract's claim of performance on par with larger multimodal models is unsupported by the reported matched comparison: Table 1 gives the fused teacher an average of 74.3 and the corresponding distilled YOLO model 54.0. Likewise, deployment claims lack inference latency, memory, parameter counts, or measurements of translator overhead. Teacher-free inference is a useful property, but it does not by itself establish minimal overhead or real-world mobile suitability.

The evaluation protocol needs clarification. Moving from oracle boxes in Table 1 to predicted boxes in Table 2 changes baseline CORe50 one-shot accuracy from 31.5 to 57.8 and iCubWorld from 33.3 to 51.2. Such increases are not necessarily impossible, but the manuscript does not explain the crop, retrieval, or sample-selection differences behind them. Episode counts, split details, and training-seed variability are also insufficiently documented; the Wilcoxon results address episode-level differences without establishing robustness across training runs.

As an Algorithms/General submission, the originality is primarily in integrating familiar feature regression, PCA whitening, prototype classification, and neighborhood-distribution matching. The paper does not adequately position its relational objective against prior relational or similarity-preserving distillation. Its ablations support utility, but the toy geometry example does not establish the claimed prevention of neural collapse, and architecture-agnostic claims are tested with only one student–teacher pairing. Together with the reproducibility and evaluation concerns, this leaves the scientific case short of acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring foundation-model representations into a compact detector for few-shot personal object recognition, without requiring teacher inference or textual inputs at deployment.

Table 2 reports meaningful improvements across four datasets. MOCHA initialized from AuXFT achieves an average score of 58.7 versus 53.8 for AuXFT and 48.6 for YOLO. The COCO-initialized variant also improves the average to 56.0, so the reported benefit is not restricted to AuXFT initialization.

The experiments include useful component analyses: visual versus multimodal supervision, translator attention, relational loss, PCA dimensionality, and initialization. Table 3 supports a contribution from the relational loss and attention, while the appendix provides additional dimensionality analyses and paired statistical comparisons.
The overall training and personalization pipeline is understandable, and the paper appropriately acknowledges training cost and limitations when scaling the personal instance inventory.
weaknesses: The central teacher representation is specified inconsistently, undermining reproducibility. Section 4.1 describes LLaVA-1.5-7B as containing CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard checkpoint uses CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 resolution. Section 3.2 also applies a shared projection to visual and textual embeddings without explaining how this corresponds to LLaVA. The hidden layer, pooled token positions, and generation settings for the semantic embedding are unspecified. Algorithm A.1 further defines this embedding as fT(ci), omitting the image conditioning central to the proposed method. These require clarification beyond cosmetic corrections.

The evaluation protocols do not adequately explain substantial differences between Tables 1 and 2. For example, YOLO's CORe50 one-shot accuracy rises from 31.5 with ground-truth boxes to 57.8 in the full detection setting, while iCubWorld rises from 33.3 to 51.2. Such changes are not necessarily impossible, but the paper attributes the distinction primarily to replacing ground-truth boxes with detections. It needs to specify any differences in feature extraction, sample selection, and scoring before the oracle analysis can be interpreted reliably.

The evidence does not sufficiently separate the proposed methodological contribution from teacher strength and additional training. Table 1 already shows that CLIP substantially outperforms the DINO teacher used by AuXFT. A matched AuXFT comparison using the same teacher features, initialization, and training budget would better establish the value of region-level transfer and the proposed alignment design. The single-modality MOCHA comparisons help, but do not resolve this confound. Under Algorithms/General, originality beyond combining established feature regression, relational matching, PCA, and prototype classification remains only partially established.

Important implementation details are missing despite the appendix: values of the new loss weights and temperature, translator dimensions and attention configuration, and precise distillation-data selection. Referring to AuXFT's implementation cannot specify these newly introduced components. Equations 7–8 also leave unclear whether self-distances are masked before softmax, which affects the stated relational objective.

The deployment claims lack quantitative support. No inference latency, parameter overhead, FLOPs, peak memory, or device measurements are reported for the retained translator and prototype classifier. Removing the teacher at inference is valuable, but does not establish the claimed minimal overhead or suitability for mobile deployment.

Several claims exceed the results. The abstract claims performance on par with larger multimodal models, yet Table 1 reports a substantial gap between the combined teacher and distilled student averages, 74.3 versus 54.0. The claimed +10.1 improvement is over undistilled YOLO; the gain over the strongest reported competitor is +4.9. Furthermore, averaging detection mAP and retrieval accuracy is a convenient summary, not a unified detection metric, and should be framed accordingly.

The experiments include useful modality, dimensionality, initialization, translator, and loss ablations. Table 3 supports the contribution of relational supervision, while Table 1 provides evidence that combining visual and language-conditioned features can improve over either alone.

This is not necessarily impossible, but the manuscript does not explain the feature, scoring, or protocol differences responsible. The abstract's claim of performance on par with larger multimodal models is also unsupported by a matched comparison; Table 1 instead shows substantial teacher–student gaps.

strengths: MOCHA addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring rich teacher representations into a compact detector for few-shot instance personalization. The frozen student and prototype-based adaptation avoid teacher inference and gradient-based adaptation on the deployment device.

The empirical improvements are substantial. In Table 2, MOCHA initialized from AuXFT improves the average score from 53.8 to 58.7, including gains of 10.3 points on PerSeg and 7.1 points on POD 5-shot. The COCO-initialized version also exceeds AuXFT on average, showing that the benefit is not entirely dependent on AuXFT initialization.

The evaluation covers four datasets, multiple detector architectures, and several personalization classifiers. Component ablations support the utility of multimodal targets, the relational loss, and the attention-based translator. Reported episodic variability and paired significance tests provide additional evidence beyond single aggregate scores.

The region-level distillation pipeline is coherent and practically motivated. Compressing cached teacher embeddings provides a plausible route to efficient training, and the measured inference overhead relative to AuXFT is modest. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges teacher computation and prototype scalability.
weaknesses: The central teacher representation is specified inconsistently, making the main contribution difficult to reproduce. Section 4.1 identifies LLaVA-1.5-7B as using CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard model uses ViT-L/14. Section 3.2 applies the same projection to visual and textual embeddings without explaining dimensional compatibility. More consequentially, Section 3.2 describes image-conditioned language features, while Algorithm 1 computes h_i = f_T(c_i), omitting the image. The manuscript should resolve whether these are multimodal hidden states, generated-description embeddings, or class-text features, and specify the extraction layer, pooled tokens, and generation settings.

The experiments do not fully separate the proposed alignment method from the stronger teacher and additional training. Table 1 shows a large advantage of CLIP over the DINO teacher used by AuXFT, but there is no AuXFT comparison using the same teacher targets. The strongest MOCHA model also continues training from AuXFT checkpoints, without an equal-budget continuation control. The COCO initialization and component ablations partly address this concern, but the attribution of the headline gain remains incomplete.

Important implementation details are missing or contradictory. The manuscript does not specify the loss weights, precise distance normalization, or translator dimensions and attention configuration. Algorithm 1 omits PCA and channel normalization when constructing distillation targets, while Appendix A.3.3 describes normalization before PCA, contrary to Equations 2–3. The scope of relational comparisons and handling of images with fewer than two objects also need clarification. These affect the actual objective rather than merely presentation.

The efficiency claims require more careful accounting. Table 6 compares 11 hours of MOCHA training from an existing AuXFT checkpoint against 50 hours for AuXFT, excluding the inherited training cost from the displayed MOCHA figure; the runs also use different epoch counts. Teacher-cache construction costs are not clearly separated. The approximately 3 ms overhead is relative to AuXFT, whereas the listed plain-detector latency is higher than both methods and unexplained. GPU measurements support modest overhead in that setting, but do not establish on-device performance.

As an Algorithms/General submission, the originality is mainly in the integration of established ingredients: feature translation, PCA-based compression, prototype classification, and pairwise relational distillation. The related-work discussion does not sufficiently position the relational objective against existing relational or similarity-preserving distillation methods. Also, no generic detection results substantiate retention of the original task, and the headline average mixes detection mAP with retrieval accuracy that accepts any matching candidate. The dataset-level gains remain meaningful, but the aggregate should not be interpreted as a uniform detection improvement.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: few-shot recognition of personal objects using a compact detector without requiring a large teacher or textual input at inference. The separation between offline distillation and lightweight personalization is practically motivated.

The reported improvements are meaningful. In Table 2, MOCHA improves the average score from 53.8 for AuXFT to 58.7, including PerSeg gains from 48.8 to 59.1 and POD 5-shot gains from 38.8 to 45.9. The COCO-initialized variant also exceeds AuXFT on average, so the evidence is not limited to the strongest initialization.

The experimental coverage is substantial: four datasets, multiple student architectures, several personalization classifiers, component ablations, and paired episodic significance tests. Table 4 supports the usefulness of both the relational loss and the attention-based translator.

The proposed combination of region-level visual and language-conditioned supervision, compressed teacher targets, and relational alignment is coherent. The paper acknowledges its relationship to AuXFT and discusses training cost and limitations of scaling prototype-based personalization.
weaknesses: The central teacher representation is specified inconsistently, which materially impedes reproducibility. Section 4.1 identifies LLaVA-1.5-7B as using CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard checkpoint uses CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336 resolution. The reported 4608-dimensional concatenation also needs reconciliation with the actual extracted features. Section 3.2 applies the same projection to visual and textual embeddings without explaining dimensional compatibility, while Algorithm 1 computes h_i = f_T(c_i), omitting the image conditioning central to the method. The exact checkpoint, extraction layer, pooled tokens, and generation procedure are needed to determine what knowledge is actually distilled.

The comparison does not adequately isolate the source of the improvement. The strongest MOCHA model starts from AuXFT weights and receives another 20 epochs of training, while the AuXFT comparator is not shown with matched additional training. Moreover, the paper itself demonstrates a large gap between CLIP and DINO teacher features in Table 1, but does not evaluate AuXFT with the same CLIP or fused teacher targets. The COCO-initialized results and modality ablations provide useful partial evidence, but a matched teacher, initialization, and training-budget comparison is needed to attribute gains to MOCHA's alignment design.

Several method-defining implementation details remain unresolved despite the appendix. These include the distillation-loss weights, channel-attention construction, distance normalization and softmax axis in the relational objective, and handling of images with fewer than two objects. Algorithm 1 computes relations within each image, whereas the broader description leaves the scope unclear. Equation 3 normalizes after PCA, but Appendix A.3.3 describes normalization before PCA; Algorithm 1 omits both operations. These choices affect the actual objective and target geometry, rather than merely presentation.

The efficiency claims require more careful accounting. Table 6 reports 11 hours for MOCHA initialized from AuXFT versus 50 hours for AuXFT, but the former inherits the latter's checkpoint and uses fewer distillation epochs. This is an incremental cost comparison, not an equivalent comparison of total training cost. Teacher-feature caching and PCA costs are not separately identified. At inference, the roughly 3 ms increase is relative to AuXFT; parameters rise from 3.9M to 4.5M and VRAM from 288.7 to 352.5 MB. Measurements on L40S hardware support modest runtime overhead, but do not establish the claimed suitability for mobile deployment.

The evidence supports a useful empirical extension more clearly than a substantial new alignment principle. Feature translation, prototype classification, PCA compression, and pairwise-distribution matching are established ingredients, and the paper does not sufficiently position the relational objective against closely related distillation methods. The ten-point synthetic experiment demonstrates optimization behavior but does not establish mitigation of feature collapse in actual detectors. Additionally, the headline +10.1 averages detection mAP and retrieval accuracy across seven settings; it should be described explicitly as a heterogeneous aggregate rather than a single detection-performance gain.

strengths: MOCHA addresses a useful computer-vision problem: few-shot recognition of personal object instances with a compact detector and no VLM inference during deployment. The separation of offline distillation from lightweight personalization is practically appealing.

The empirical gains are meaningful. In Table 2, MOCHA improves the reported average from 53.8 for AuXFT to 58.7, including improvements from 48.8 to 59.1 on PerSeg and from 38.8 to 45.9 on POD 5-shot. The COCO-initialized version also exceeds AuXFT on average, so the evidence is not limited to the configuration initialized from AuXFT.

The experiments cover four datasets, multiple detector architectures, and several few-shot classifiers. Table 4 supports the usefulness of relational supervision and translator attention, while the modality ablations provide evidence that combining visual and language-conditioned features improves average performance.

The frozen teacher, compressed region descriptors, and prototype-based personalization form a coherent pipeline. The appendix provides additional ablations, computational measurements, and an explicit discussion of training cost and scalability limitations.
weaknesses: The central teacher representation is insufficiently specified and inconsistently described. Section 4.1 identifies LLaVA-1.5-7B's visual encoder as CLIP ViT-B/32, whereas the standard checkpoint uses ViT-L/14. Section 3.2 applies the same projection to visual and textual embeddings without explaining dimensional compatibility, and Algorithm 1 writes h_i = f_T(c_i), omitting image conditioning. The hidden layer, pooled token positions, and generation settings are also unspecified. These issues materially hinder reproduction of the main contribution.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed distillation mechanism from teacher quality and additional training. Table 1 already shows a large advantage for CLIP over AuXFT's DINO teacher. The strongest MOCHA model then starts from AuXFT and receives further training. A matched-teacher AuXFT comparison and an equal-budget continued-training control would better establish the source of the gains. The COCO-initialized results mitigate, but do not eliminate, this concern.

Important implementation details remain unclear despite the appendix: the loss weights, precise translator configuration, distance normalization, and handling of images with fewer than two objects for the relational loss. The appendix also describes channel normalization as occurring before PCA, contradicting Equations 2–3. Referring to AuXFT's implementation does not resolve choices specific to MOCHA.

The efficiency claims need more careful accounting. Table 6 compares 11 hours of MOCHA training from an existing AuXFT checkpoint against 50 hours for AuXFT, without incorporating the prerequisite checkpoint cost into the comparison. Teacher extraction and caching costs should be explicitly itemized. The approximately 3 ms overhead is relative to AuXFT, and measurements on an L40S do not directly establish mobile-device performance.

The contribution is primarily an integration of established techniques—feature translation, PCA compression, pointwise distillation, relational matching, and prototypical classification—so its strongest case is empirical. Some broader claims exceed that evidence: preservation of original generic detection performance is not evaluated, and the headline average mixes detection mAP with a retrieval metric that accepts any matching candidate. These limitations warrant narrower claims, although they do not negate the reported benchmark improvements.
